title: "Different learners, the same estimate?"
subtitle: "An R companion to Susan’s Causal Roadmap tutorial"
output:

---

Susan asks how five-year mortality would change under a shorter radiation schedule for older or frailer patients eligible for either schedule. A negative risk difference means fewer deaths under the shorter schedule. The main roadmap’s primary outcome is restricted mean survival time through five years, the average time alive during that window. This exercise uses a fully ascertained binary outcome so every step can be checked by hand.

Open this file in RStudio and select **Knit**, or run `rmarkdown::render("analysis.Rmd")` in its directory. All data are synthetic. The estimators use base R. The tables use **knitr**.

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, collapse = FALSE, error = FALSE, comment = "#>")
options(knitr.kable.NA = "")
```

## Terms used in the calculations

| Term | Meaning in this example |
| --- | --- |
| Estimand, estimator, estimate | The estimand specifies whose five-year risks to compare. The estimator is the rule for combining the records. The estimate is the resulting number. |
| Base learner and meta-learner | A base learner fits a prediction, such as a regression for mortality. A meta-learner arranges prediction fits to estimate how a treatment effect varies. |
| Outcome model and propensity | The outcome model predicts mortality for a given schedule and frailty. The propensity is the chance of receiving the short schedule at that frailty. Both help estimate the causal contrast. |
| Standardization | Average predicted risks for both schedules using the same patients and the same frailty mix. |
| Cross-fitting | Train the prediction models on some records and use them to score other records. Rotate the held-out group so every record is scored once. |

## The records Susan has

The 5,000 training records contain baseline frailty (`L`, 1 for higher), received schedule (`A`, 1 for short), and death by five years (`Y`, 1 for death). The causal interpretation assumes consistent treatment definitions, exchangeability given baseline frailty, and both schedules available in each target stratum. These are features of the teaching example. Applying it to clinical records would require clinical justification.

```{r counts}
cells <- data.frame(
  L = c(0L, 0L, 1L, 1L), A = c(0L, 1L, 0L, 1L),
  patients = c(900L, 2100L, 1500L, 500L),
  deaths = c(180L, 462L, 600L, 125L)
)
expand_records <- function(cells) {
  data.frame(
    L = rep(cells$L, cells$patients),
    A = rep(cells$A, cells$patients),
    Y = as.integer(sequence(cells$patients) <= rep(cells$deaths, cells$patients))
  )
}
train <- expand_records(cells)
profiles <- data.frame(L = 0:1)
profile_names <- c("Lower frailty", "Higher frailty")
stopifnot(nrow(train) == 5000L)
knitr::kable(cells)
```

The crude comparison uses the two groups as observed. More higher-frailty people received the standard schedule.

```{r observed}
arm_risk <- tapply(train$Y, train$A, mean)
round(100 * c(standard = unname(arm_risk["0"]), short = unname(arm_risk["1"]),
              difference = unname(arm_risk["1"] - arm_risk["0"])), 2)
```

## S and T ask for the same two risks

The S-learner fits one logistic regression. The schedule-by-frailty interaction gives each arm its own intercept and slope. The T-learner fits a separate regression in each arm. Both predict each baseline profile under each schedule. The difference between those conditional mean risks estimates the **conditional average treatment effect** (CATE).

```{r two-risks}
s_full <- glm(Y ~ A * L, data = train, family = binomial())
s_shared <- glm(Y ~ A + L, data = train, family = binomial())
t_standard <- glm(Y ~ L, data = train, subset = A == 0L, family = binomial())
t_short <- glm(Y ~ L, data = train, subset = A == 1L, family = binomial())

risk <- function(fit, rows) unname(predict(fit, newdata = rows, type = "response"))
standard <- transform(profiles, A = 0L)
short <- transform(profiles, A = 1L)
s0 <- risk(s_full, standard)
s1 <- risk(s_full, short)
t0 <- risk(t_standard, profiles)
t1 <- risk(t_short, profiles)
shared0 <- risk(s_shared, standard)
shared1 <- risk(s_shared, short)

knitr::kable(data.frame(profile = profile_names,
  standard_pct = 100*t0, short_pct = 100*t1,
  S_difference_pp = 100*(s1 - s0), T_difference_pp = 100*(t1 - t0),
  shared_S_difference_pp = 100*(shared1 - shared0)), digits = 2)
stopifnot(max(abs(s0 - t0), abs(s1 - t1)) < 1e-6)
```

Under the unpenalized, fully interacted fit, the likelihood separates into the two arm-specific fits, so S and T agree. Removing the interaction gives both frailty groups a common schedule odds ratio. Read the lower-frailty row again. The estimated risk difference changes sign.

## One outcome per patient

The six display patients are held out of model fitting. Consistency tells Susan which potential outcome she observed. The paired outcome under the other schedule stays blank. The two predicted risks apply to people with that baseline profile.

```{r display-patients}
display <- data.frame(
  id = sprintf("P%02d", 1:6), L = c(0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1),
  A = c(0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0), Y = c(0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0)
)
display$observed_under_standard <- ifelse(display$A == 0L, display$Y, NA_integer_)
display$observed_under_short <- ifelse(display$A == 1L, display$Y, NA_integer_)
display$risk_standard <- risk(t_standard, display)
display$risk_short <- risk(t_short, display)
knitr::kable(display, digits = 2)
```

## X brings the observed outcome back

In the short arm, the pseudo-effect is observed outcome minus fitted standard risk. In the standard arm it is fitted short risk minus observed outcome. Both use the same direction. For a higher-frailty death these are +0.60 (P04) and −0.75 (P05). The two large, noisy pseudo-effects explain why the next step regresses them on baseline characteristics.

```{r x-learner}
pseudo_effect <- function(rows) {
  observed <- rows[["Y"]]
  ifelse(rows[["A"]] == 1L, observed - risk(t_standard, rows),
                           risk(t_short, rows) - observed)
}
train$D <- pseudo_effect(train)
display$D <- pseudo_effect(display)
stopifnot(abs(display$D[4] - 0.60) < 1e-6,
          abs(display$D[5] + 0.75) < 1e-6)

x_standard <- lm(D ~ L, data = train, subset = A == 0L)
x_short <- lm(D ~ L, data = train, subset = A == 1L)
tau0 <- unname(predict(x_standard, profiles))
tau1 <- unname(predict(x_short, profiles))
e <- risk(glm(A ~ L, data = train, family = binomial()), profiles)
tau_x <- e*tau0 + (1 - e)*tau1
knitr::kable(data.frame(profile = profile_names, probability_short = e,
  from_standard_pp = 100*tau0, from_short_pp = 100*tau1,
  X_difference_pp = 100*tau_x), digits = 2)
stopifnot(max(abs(tau_x - (t1 - t0))) < 1e-6)
```

Here each stage fits a separate mean in each frailty stratum, so both second-stage fits reproduce the same conditional difference. Try the blend with two *hypothetical* second-stage predictions that disagree. At a probability of short of 0.25, the standard-arm fit gets weight 0.25. The short-arm fit uses the opposite arm’s prediction of standard risk.

```{r unequal-blend}
example_blend <- 0.25*(-0.02) + (1 - 0.25)*(-0.06)
stopifnot(abs(example_blend + 0.05) < 1e-8)
100*example_blend
```

## Whose average?

First standardize to all 5,000 eligible patients (ATE). Then use the baseline distribution of the 2,600 short-schedule recipients (ATT). Both sets of weights use the training cohort. Changing which six display patients are shown leaves these weights intact.

```{r standardization}
weights <- rbind(
  ATE = as.numeric(prop.table(table(train$L))),
  ATT = as.numeric(prop.table(table(train$L[train$A == 1L])))
)
risk_columns <- cbind(standard = t0, short = t1, S = s1 - s0,
  T = t1 - t0, X = tau_x, shared_S = shared1 - shared0)
estimates <- weights %*% risk_columns
knitr::kable(100*estimates, digits = 2,
  caption = "Two arm risks in percent, followed by four risk differences in percentage points.")
stopifnot(max(abs(estimates["ATE", c("S", "T", "X")] + 0.048)) < 1e-6,
          max(abs(estimates["ATT", c("S", "T", "X")] + 33/2600)) < 1e-6,
          abs(unname(arm_risk["1"] - arm_risk["0"]) + 0.0992307692) < 1e-6)
```

The fully interacted S-learner, T-learner and X-learner all estimate **+2 points** in lower-frailty patients and **−15 points** in higher-frailty patients. For the full cohort, 60% have lower frailty and 40% higher. The shared estimate is **−4.80 percentage points**. Among short recipients, 2,100 of 2,600 have lower frailty, giving **−1.27 points**. The S-learner with a shared log-odds treatment effect gives different estimates in the last column.

## TMLE and double machine learning across the cohort

Susan keeps the all-eligible target fixed. Targeted maximum likelihood estimation (TMLE) updates predictions across both frailty groups. Double machine learning (DML) rotates training and scoring through groups of records. Each method below uses the 5,000 fitting records. The separate six-row illustration belongs to the S-, T- and X-learner worksheet.

### Target the difference with TMLE

The lower-frailty group contributes 3,000 records and the higher-frailty group contributes 2,000. Pool the schedules within each group to get a starting risk under either schedule. The starting cohort difference is zero. Estimate the probability of short, `e`, within each group. Use it to weight signed prediction errors through a **clever covariate** `H`, equal to `1/e` on short and `-1/(1-e)` on standard. Fit one coefficient, `epsilon`, across all 5,000 records by logistic regression with the initial log odds as an offset and no intercept. Apply that update under both schedules in each group.

```{r targeting}
group <- train[["L"]] + 1L
arm <- train[["A"]]
observed <- train[["Y"]]
q_initial <- as.numeric(tapply(observed, group, mean))
g_full <- as.numeric(tapply(arm, group, mean))
h0 <- -1 / (1 - g_full)
h1 <- 1 / g_full
H <- ifelse(arm == 1L, h1[group], h0[group])
initial_log_odds <- qlogis(q_initial[group])
fluctuation <- glm(observed ~ 0 + H + offset(initial_log_odds),
                   family = binomial(), control = glm.control(epsilon = 1e-12))
epsilon <- unname(coef(fluctuation)[1])
qstar0 <- plogis(qlogis(q_initial) + epsilon * h0)
qstar1 <- plogis(qlogis(q_initial) + epsilon * h1)
qstar_obs <- ifelse(arm == 1L, qstar1[group], qstar0[group])
tmle_ate <- mean(qstar1[group] - qstar0[group])
score_before <- mean(H * (observed - q_initial[group]))
score_after <- mean(H * (observed - qstar_obs))
cohort_n <- as.numeric(table(group))
knitr::kable(data.frame(profile_names, cohort_n, 100*g_full, 100*q_initial,
                       100*qstar0, 100*qstar1), digits = 3,
             col.names = c("Frailty", "Patients", "Received short (%)", "Starting risk (%)",
                           "Updated standard (%)", "Updated short (%)"))
stopifnot(abs(epsilon + 0.049149193627) < 1e-9, abs(score_before + 0.048) < 1e-9,
          abs(score_after) < 1e-9, abs(tmle_ate + 0.048) < 1e-9)
```

The fitted coefficient is −0.049149. Check its effect in two ways. First, take the cohort mean of `H * (observed - fitted risk)` under the schedule actually received. It moves from **−0.048 to zero**. Second, average the updated risks under each schedule using the same 60% lower-frailty and 40% higher-frailty mix.

```{r targeting-summary}
starting_risk <- weighted.mean(q_initial, cohort_n)
tmle_standard <- weighted.mean(qstar0, cohort_n)
tmle_short <- weighted.mean(qstar1, cohort_n)
knitr::kable(data.frame(step = c("Before update", "After update"),
                       standard = 100*c(starting_risk, tmle_standard),
                       short = 100*c(starting_risk, tmle_short),
                       difference = 100*c(0, tmle_short - tmle_standard),
                       score = c(score_before, score_after)), digits = c(0, 5, 5, 2, 3),
             col.names = c("Cohort fit", "Standard mortality (%)", "Short mortality (%)",
                           "Difference (points)", "Mean H × residual"))
stopifnot(abs(starting_risk - 0.2734) < 1e-9,
          abs(tmle_short - tmle_standard - tmle_ate) < 1e-9)
```

The two standardized risks are **24.88169% on short and 29.68169% on standard**, a difference of **−4.80 points**. This single coefficient targets the population difference. Individual arm means and frailty contrasts can differ from the S/T fit. [Schuler and Rose on TMLE for observational data](https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kww165) · [Balzer, Petersen and van der Laan on targeting a difference](https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.6965)

### Train on four folds, score on the fifth

For double machine learning (DML), split every frailty-by-schedule cell into five equal parts. Within a cell of size `n`, label the synthetic rows `j = 0, ..., n-1` in their original order. The fixed permutation `(37*j + 17) %% n` uses only the row label and cell size. The first fifth of permuted ranks goes to fold 1, and so on. Each fold contains 1,000 distinct fitting records and leaves 4,000 to train its models. Outcomes play no part in assigning folds. This is a reproducible stratified teaching split.

```{r honest-folds}
make_folds <- function(n) {
  j <- seq_len(n) - 1L
  rank <- (37L * j + 17L) %% n
  stopifnot(length(unique(rank)) == n)
  1L + (5L * rank) %/% n
}
fold <- unlist(lapply(cells[["patients"]], make_folds), use.names = FALSE)
stopifnot(all(table(fold) == 1000L))
fit_profiles <- function(rows) {
  frailty <- rows[["L"]]
  a <- rows[["A"]]
  y <- rows[["Y"]]
  data.frame(e = as.numeric(tapply(a, frailty, mean)),
             q0 = as.numeric(tapply(y[a == 0L], frailty[a == 0L], mean)),
             q1 = as.numeric(tapply(y[a == 1L], frailty[a == 1L], mean)),
             m = as.numeric(tapply(y, frailty, mean)))
}
fits <- vector("list", 5)
out_of_fold <- data.frame(e = rep(NA_real_, nrow(train)), q0 = NA_real_,
                          q1 = NA_real_, m = NA_real_)
for (k in seq_along(fits)) {
  held <- fold == k
  fits[[k]] <- fit_profiles(train[!held, ])
  out_of_fold[held, ] <- fits[[k]][group[held], ]
}
stopifnot(!anyNA(out_of_fold), abs(fits[[1]]$q0[2] - 479/1200) < 1e-12)
```

In each rotation, use the four training folds to fit two mortality risks and the probability of short by frailty. Predict both risks across the 1,000 held-out records. Their mean short-minus-standard difference is the **starting contrast**. Compare observed mortality to predicted mortality under the received schedule in that same fold. The mean signed, inverse-probability-weighted discrepancy is the **correction**. Adding it to the starting contrast gives the fold’s augmented inverse probability weighting (AIPW) estimate in the interactive regression model (IRM).

```{r dml-ate}
q_received <- ifelse(arm == 1L, out_of_fold[["q1"]], out_of_fold[["q0"]])
h_held <- ifelse(arm == 1L, 1 / out_of_fold[["e"]], -1 / (1 - out_of_fold[["e"]]))
initial_difference <- out_of_fold[["q1"]] - out_of_fold[["q0"]]
correction <- h_held * (observed - q_received)
contribution <- initial_difference + correction
irm_ate <- mean(contribution)
fold_n <- as.integer(table(fold))
mean_by_fold <- function(x) as.numeric(tapply(x, fold, mean))
fold_results <- data.frame(held = as.character(seq_along(fold_n)),
                           trained = nrow(train) - fold_n, scored = fold_n,
                           start = mean_by_fold(initial_difference),
                           correction = mean_by_fold(correction), result = mean_by_fold(contribution))
pooled <- data.frame(held = "All folds", trained = NA_integer_, scored = sum(fold_n),
                     start = weighted.mean(fold_results$start, fold_n),
                     correction = weighted.mean(fold_results$correction, fold_n),
                     result = weighted.mean(fold_results$result, fold_n))
report <- rbind(fold_results, pooled)
knitr::kable(transform(report, start = 100*start, correction = 100*correction,
                      result = 100*result), digits = c(0, 0, 0, 3, 3, 3),
             col.names = c("Scored fold", "Trained on", "Scored", "Starting contrast (pp)",
                           "Mean correction (pp)", "Fold or cohort estimate (pp)"))
stopifnot(sum(fold_n) == nrow(train),
          max(abs(report$start + report$correction - report$result)) < 1e-12,
          abs(pooled$start + 0.048) < 1e-9, abs(pooled$correction) < 1e-9,
          abs(pooled$result - irm_ate) < 1e-9, abs(irm_ate + 0.048) < 1e-9)
```

In fold 1 the initial difference is −4.633 points, the correction is −0.833 points and the resulting estimate is −5.467 points (rounded). The final row weights each fold by its number of scored records. Every record is scored once. The nonzero fold corrections cancel in this balanced synthetic design, giving **−4.80 points** for all 5,000 patients. Other datasets and nuisance fits can yield a nonzero overall correction and different finite-sample estimates from TMLE. [Chernozhukov et al., sections 3–5](https://doi.org/10.1111/ectj.12097) · [DoubleML score equations](https://docs.doubleml.org/stable/guide/scores.html)

### A separate partially linear comparison

Partially linear regression (PLR) uses two residuals from held-out predictions. Subtract the predicted chance of short from the schedule received and subtract the mortality predicted from frailty alone from the outcome. Pool the outcome-by-treatment residual cross-products across all five folds, and divide once by the pooled squared treatment residuals. In this design each fold has the same fraction treated within each frailty group, so the pooled slope exactly matches the ordinary Frisch–Waugh–Lovell (FWL) result from regressing `Y` on `A` and frailty.

```{r dml-plr}
treatment_residual <- arm - out_of_fold[["e"]]
outcome_residual <- observed - out_of_fold[["m"]]
cross_products <- tapply(treatment_residual * outcome_residual, fold, sum)
squared_treatment <- tapply(treatment_residual^2, fold, sum)
num <- sum(cross_products)
den <- sum(squared_treatment)
plr <- num / den
fwl <- unname(coef(lm(Y ~ A + factor(L), data = train))["A"])
overlap_mass <- cohort_n * g_full * (1 - g_full)
overlap_weight <- overlap_mass / sum(overlap_mass)
overlap_target <- sum(overlap_weight * (t1 - t0))
knitr::kable(data.frame(scored = nrow(train), cross_product = num, squared_treatment = den,
                       plr = 100*plr, fwl = 100*fwl), digits = c(0, 2, 0, 5, 5),
             col.names = c("Scored records", "Sum of residual cross-products",
                           "Sum of squared treatment residuals", "PLR slope (pp)", "OLS / FWL (pp)"))
stopifnot(abs(num + 43.65) < 1e-9, abs(den - 1005) < 1e-9,
          max(abs(plr - fwl), abs(plr - overlap_target)) < 1e-9,
          abs(plr - irm_ate) > 0.004)
```

The residualized slope is −43.65 / 1,005 = −0.0434328, or **−4.34328 percentage points**. With a binary schedule and heterogeneous effects, the partially linear projection weights each frailty group in proportion to its frequency times `e * (1-e)`. The two overlap masses are 630 and 375. The lower-frailty group therefore gets 62.69% of the weight in this projection and 60% in Susan’s all-eligible ATE. TMLE uses its clever covariate to target an outcome regression. Treatment residualization belongs to the PLR calculation. [Why a partially linear model weights overlap](https://docs.doubleml.org/stable/examples/py_double_ml_plm_irm_hetfx.html)

## What if one schedule is unavailable?

In another synthetic clinic, a clinical rule makes the short schedule unavailable to every higher-frailty patient. Hold the lower-frailty data fixed. Keep the unavailable risk and full-target contrast unresolved. If Susan asks a new question about the 3,000 lower-frailty patients, those patients contribute evidence for both schedules.

```{r support}
second_clinic <- cells
high <- second_clinic$L == 1L
second_clinic$patients[high] <- c(2000L, 0L)
second_clinic$deaths[high] <- c(800L, 0L)

counts <- xtabs(patients ~ L + A, data = second_clinic)
deaths <- xtabs(deaths ~ L + A, data = second_clinic)
risks <- deaths / counts
risks[counts == 0] <- NA_real_
supported <- counts[, "0"] > 0 & counts[, "1"] > 0
difference <- risks[, "1"] - risks[, "0"]
target_n <- rowSums(counts)
full_target <- weighted.mean(difference, target_n)
shared_target <- weighted.mean(difference[supported], target_n[supported])
stopifnot(is.na(full_target), sum(target_n[supported]) == 3000L,
          abs(shared_target - 0.02) < 1e-8)
knitr::kable(data.frame(profile = profile_names,
  standard_n = as.integer(counts[, "0"]), short_n = as.integer(counts[, "1"]),
  difference_pp = as.numeric(100*difference)), digits = 2)
```

The revised target has a **+2 percentage-point** estimated risk difference. In real data, an empty sample cell can also arise by chance. Susan would ask the clinicians whether both schedules were realistic options before redefining whom her conclusion covers.

## Read the worksheet alongside the paper

Künzel and colleagues write $W$ for the schedule (`A` in this notebook) and $X$ for the baseline covariates (`L` for frailty here). Their $\tau(x)$ is the mean difference in outcomes for patients with baseline profile $x$. For this binary outcome it is a five-year mortality risk difference, short minus standard.

| In the notebook | On printed page 4158 |
| --- | --- |
| T fits one risk model in each arm. S fits one model and predicts twice. | Equation 3 (T) and equation 4 (S) |
| X fits risks, imputes a signed difference for each training record, then fits those differences within each arm. | Equations 5–6 (risks), 7 (short-arm pseudo-outcome), and 8 (standard-arm pseudo-outcome) |
| X averages the two fitted effects at the same frailty profile. | Equation 9, with the estimated propensity as the blending weight here |

The final ATE and ATT calculation in this notebook averages the profile effects over the chosen patients. Open the [paper at the equations](https://ishuryak.github.io/causal-roadmap-primer/preview/estimators/kunzel-2019.pdf#page=3) or read the [accessible full-text article](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6410831/).
